{{Short description|Sheaf consisting of modules on a ringed space; generalizing vector bundles}}{{Technical|date=November 2023}}
In mathematics, a '''sheaf of ''O''-modules''' or simply an '''''O''-module''' over a [[ringed space]] (''X'', ''O'') is a [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]] of [[abelian groups]] ''F'' such that, for any open subset ''U'' of ''X'', ''F''(''U'') is an ''O''(''U'')-module and the restriction maps ''F''(''U'')&nbsp;→&nbsp;''F''(''V'') are compatible with the restriction maps ''O''(''U'')&nbsp;→&nbsp;''O''(''V''): the restriction of ''fs'' is the restriction of ''f'' times the restriction of ''s'' for any ''f'' in ''O''(''U'') and ''s'' in ''F''(''U'').

The standard case is when ''X'' is a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] and ''O'' its structure sheaf. If ''O'' is the [[constant sheaf]] <math>\underline{\mathbf{Z}}</math>, then a sheaf of ''O''-modules is the same as a [[sheaf of abelian groups]] (i.e., an '''abelian sheaf''').

If ''X'' is the [[prime spectrum]] of a ring ''R'', then any ''R''-module defines an ''O''<sub>''X''</sub>-module (called an '''associated sheaf''') in a natural way. Similarly, if ''R'' is a [[graded ring]] and ''X'' is the [[Proj construction|Proj]] of ''R'', then any graded module defines an ''O''<sub>''X''</sub>-module in a natural way. ''O''-modules arising in such a fashion are examples of [[quasi-coherent sheaves]], and in fact, on affine or projective schemes, all quasi-coherent sheaves are obtained this way.

Sheaves of modules over a ringed space form an [[abelian category]].<ref>Vakil, [http://math.stanford.edu/~vakil/216blog/FOAGjun1113public.pdf Math 216: Foundations of algebraic geometry], 2.5.</ref> Moreover, this category has [[enough injectives]],<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|loc=Ch. III, Proposition 2.2.}}</ref> and consequently one can and does define the [[sheaf cohomology]] <math>\operatorname{H}^i(X, -)</math> as the ''i''-th [[right derived functor]] of the [[global section functor]] <math>\Gamma(X, -)</math>.<ref>This cohomology functor coincides with the right derived functor of the global section functor in the category of abelian sheaves; cf. {{harvnb|Hartshorne|loc=Ch. III, Proposition 2.6.}}</ref>

== Examples ==
*Given a ringed space (''X'', ''O''), if ''F'' is an ''O''-submodule of ''O'', then it is called the sheaf of ideals or [[ideal sheaf]] of ''O'', since for each open subset ''U'' of ''X'', ''F''(''U'') is an [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of the ring ''O''(''U'').
*Let ''X'' be a [[smooth variety]] of dimension ''n''. Then the [[tangent sheaf]] of ''X'' is the dual of the [[cotangent sheaf]] <math>\Omega_X</math> and the [[canonical sheaf]] <math>\omega_X</math> is the ''n''-th exterior power ([[determinant line bundle|determinant]]) of <math>\Omega_X</math>.
*A [[sheaf of algebras]] is a sheaf of modules that is also a sheaf of rings.

== Operations ==
Let (''X'', ''O'') be a ringed space. If ''F'' and ''G'' are ''O''-modules, then their tensor product, denoted by
:<math>F \otimes_O G</math> or <math>F \otimes G</math>,
is the ''O''-module that is the sheaf associated to the presheaf <math>U \mapsto F(U) \otimes_{O(U)} G(U).</math> (To see that [[Sheaf (mathematics)#Turning a presheaf into a sheaf|sheafification]] cannot be avoided, compute the global sections of <math>O(1) \otimes O(-1) = O</math> where ''O''(1) is [[Serre's twisting sheaf]] on a projective space.)

Similarly, if ''F'' and ''G'' are ''O''-modules, then
:<math>\mathcal{H}om_O(F, G)</math>
denotes the ''O''-module that is the sheaf <math>U \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{O|_U}(F|_U, G|_U)</math>.<ref>There is a canonical homomorphism:
:<math>\mathcal{H}om_O(F, O)_x \to \operatorname{Hom}_{O_x} (F_x, O_x),</math>
which is an isomorphism if ''F'' is of finite presentation (EGA, Ch. 0, 5.2.6.)</ref> In particular, the ''O''-module
:<math>\mathcal{H}om_O(F, O)</math>
is called the '''dual module''' of ''F'' and is denoted by <math>\check F</math>. Note: for any ''O''-modules ''E'', ''F'', there is a canonical homomorphism
:<math>\check{E} \otimes F \to \mathcal{H}om_O(E, F)</math>,
which is an isomorphism if ''E'' is a [[locally free sheaf]] of finite rank. In particular, if ''L'' is locally free of rank one (such ''L'' is called an [[invertible sheaf]] or a [[line bundle]]),<ref>For coherent sheaves, having a tensor inverse is the same as being locally free of rank one; in fact, there is the following fact: if <math>F \otimes G \simeq O</math> and if ''F'' is coherent, then ''F'', ''G'' are locally free of rank one. (cf. EGA, Ch 0, 5.4.3.)</ref> then this reads:
:<math>\check{L} \otimes L \simeq O,</math>
implying the isomorphism classes of invertible sheaves form a group. This group is called the [[Picard group]] of ''X'' and is canonically identified with the first cohomology group <math>\operatorname{H}^1(X, \mathcal{O}^*)</math> (by the standard argument with [[Čech cohomology]]).

If ''E'' is a locally free sheaf of finite rank, then there is an ''O''-linear map <math>\check{E} \otimes E \simeq \operatorname{End}_O(E) \to O</math> given by the pairing; it is called the [[Categorical trace|trace map]] of ''E''.

For any ''O''-module ''F'', the [[tensor algebra]], [[exterior algebra]] and [[symmetric algebra]] of ''F'' are defined in the same way. For example, the ''k''-th exterior power
:<math>\bigwedge^k F</math>
is the sheaf associated to the presheaf <math display="inline">U \mapsto \bigwedge^k_{O(U)} F(U)</math>. If ''F'' is locally free of rank ''n'', then <math display="inline">\bigwedge^n F</math> is called the [[determinant line bundle]] (though technically [[invertible sheaf]]) of ''F'', denoted by det(''F''). There is a natural perfect pairing:
:<math>\bigwedge^r F \otimes \bigwedge^{n-r} F \to \det(F).</math>

Let ''f'': (''X'', ''O'') →(''X{{'}}'', ''O{{'}}'') be a morphism of ringed spaces. If ''F'' is an ''O''-module, then the [[direct image sheaf]] <math>f_* F</math> is an ''O{{'}}''-module through the natural map ''O{{'}}'' →''f''<sub>*</sub>''O'' (such a natural map is part of the data of a morphism of ringed spaces.)

If ''G'' is an ''O{{'}}''-module, then the module inverse image <math>f^* G</math> of ''G'' is the ''O''-module given as the tensor product of modules:
:<math>f^{-1} G \otimes_{f^{-1} O'} O</math>
where <math>f^{-1} G</math> is the [[inverse image sheaf]] of ''G'' and <math>f^{-1} O' \to O</math> is obtained from <math>O' \to f_* O</math> by [[adjoint functor|adjuction]].

There is an adjoint relation between <math>f_*</math> and <math>f^*</math>: for any ''O''-module ''F'' and ''O<nowiki>'</nowiki>''-module ''G'',
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}_{O}(f^* G, F) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{O'}(G, f_*F)</math>
as abelian group. There is also the [[projection formula]]: for an ''O''-module ''F'' and a locally free ''O<nowiki>'</nowiki>''-module ''E'' of finite rank,
:<math>f_*(F \otimes f^*E) \simeq f_* F \otimes E.</math>

== Properties ==
{{anchor|Generated by global sections}}
Let (''X'', ''O'') be a ringed space. An ''O''-module ''F'' is said to be '''generated by global sections''' if there is a surjection of ''O''-modules:
:<math>\bigoplus_{i \in I} O \to F \to 0.</math>
Explicitly, this means that there are global sections ''s''<sub>''i''</sub> of ''F'' such that the images of ''s''<sub>''i''</sub> in each stalk ''F''<sub>''x''</sub> generate ''F''<sub>''x''</sub> as ''O''<sub>''x''</sub>-module.

An example of such a sheaf is that associated in [[algebraic geometry]] to an ''R''-module ''M'', ''R'' being any [[commutative ring]], on the [[spectrum of a ring]] ''Spec''(''R'').
Another example: according to [[Cartan's theorem A]], any [[coherent sheaf]] on a [[Stein manifold]] is spanned by global sections. (cf. Serre's theorem A below.) In the theory of [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]], a related notion is [[ample line bundle]]. (For example, if ''L'' is an ample line bundle, some power of it is generated by global sections.)

An injective ''O''-module is [[flasque sheaf|flasque]] (i.e., all restrictions maps ''F''(''U'') → ''F''(''V'') are surjective).<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|loc=Ch III, Lemma 2.4.}}</ref> Since a flasque sheaf is acyclic in the category of abelian sheaves, this implies that the ''i''-th right derived functor of the global section functor <math>\Gamma(X, -)</math> in the category of ''O''-modules coincides with the usual ''i''-th sheaf cohomology in the category of abelian sheaves.<ref>see also: https://math.stackexchange.com/q/447234</ref><!--A little imprecise: Thus, for example, one can use [[Čech cohomology]] to compute cohomology of ''X'' with coefficients in ''O''-modules.-->

== Sheaf associated to a module ==
Let <math>M</math> be a module over a ring <math>A</math>. Put <math>X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)</math> and write <math>D(f) = \{ f \ne 0 \} = \operatorname{Spec}(A[f^{-1}])</math>. For each pair <math>D(f) \subseteq D(g)</math>, by the [[universal property]] of localization, there is a natural map
:<math>\rho_{g, f}: M[g^{-1}] \to M[f^{-1}]</math>
having the property that <math>\rho_{g, f} = \rho_{g, h} \circ \rho_{h, f}</math>. Then
:<math>D(f) \mapsto M[f^{-1}]</math>
is a contravariant functor from the category whose objects are the sets ''D''(''f'') and morphisms the inclusions of sets to the [[category of abelian groups]]. One can show<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|loc=Ch. II, Proposition 5.1.}}</ref>  it is in fact a [[B-sheaf]] (i.e., it satisfies the gluing axiom) and thus defines the sheaf <math>\widetilde{M}</math> on ''X'' called the sheaf associated to ''M''.

The most basic example is the structure sheaf on ''X''; i.e., <math>\mathcal{O}_X = \widetilde{A}</math>. Moreover, <math>\widetilde{M}</math> has the structure of <math>\mathcal{O}_X = \widetilde{A}</math>-module and thus one gets the [[exact functor]] <math>M \mapsto \widetilde{M}</math> from Mod<sub>''A''</sub>, the [[category of modules]] over ''A'' to the category of modules over <math>\mathcal{O}_X</math>. It defines an [[Equivalence of categories|equivalence]] from Mod<sub>''A''</sub> to the category of [[quasi-coherent sheaves]] on ''X'', with the inverse <math>\Gamma(X, -)</math>, the [[global section functor]]. When ''X'' is [[Noetherian scheme|Noetherian]], the functor is an equivalence from the category of finitely generated ''A''-modules to the category of coherent sheaves on ''X''.

The construction has the following properties: for any ''A''-modules ''M'', ''N'', and any morphism <math>\varphi:M\to N</math>,
*<math>M[f^{-1}]^{\sim} = \widetilde{M}|_{D(f)}</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|EGA I|1971|loc=Ch. I, Proposition 1.3.6.}}</ref>
*For any prime ideal ''p'' of ''A'', <math>\widetilde{M}_p \simeq M_p</math> as ''O''<sub>''p''</sub> = ''A''<sub>''p''</sub>-module.
*<math>(M \otimes_A N)^{\sim} \simeq \widetilde{M} \otimes_{\widetilde{A}} \widetilde{N}</math>.<ref name="Corollary 1.3.12.">{{harvnb|EGA I|1971|loc=Ch. I, Corollaire 1.3.12.}}</ref>
*If ''M'' is [[finitely presented module|finitely presented]], <math>\operatorname{Hom}_A(M, N)^{\sim} \simeq \mathcal{H}om_{\widetilde{A}}(\widetilde{M}, \widetilde{N})</math>.<ref name="Corollary 1.3.12." />
*<math>\operatorname{Hom}_A(M, N) \simeq \Gamma(X, \mathcal{H}om_{\widetilde{A}}(\widetilde{M}, \widetilde{N}))</math>, since the equivalence between Mod<sub>''A''</sub> and the category of quasi-coherent sheaves on ''X''.
*<math>(\varinjlim M_i)^{\sim} \simeq \varinjlim \widetilde{M_i}</math>;<ref>{{harvnb|EGA I|1971|loc=Ch. I, Corollaire 1.3.9.}}</ref> in particular, taking a direct sum and ~ commute.
*A sequence of ''A''-modules is exact if and only if the induced sequence by <math>\sim</math> is exact. In particular, <math>(\ker(\varphi))^{\sim}=\ker(\widetilde{\varphi}), (\operatorname{coker}(\varphi))^{\sim}=\operatorname{coker}(\widetilde{\varphi}), (\operatorname{im}(\varphi))^{\sim}=\operatorname{im}(\widetilde{\varphi})</math>.

== Sheaf associated to a graded module ==
There is a graded analog of the construction and equivalence in the preceding section. Let ''R'' be a graded ring generated by degree-one elements as ''R''<sub>0</sub>-algebra (''R''<sub>0</sub> means the degree-zero piece) and ''M'' a graded ''R''-module. Let ''X'' be the [[Proj construction|Proj]] of ''R'' (so ''X'' is a [[projective scheme]] if ''R'' is [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]]). Then there is an ''O''-module <math>\widetilde{M}</math> such that for any homogeneous element ''f'' of positive degree of ''R'', there is a natural isomorphism
:<math>\widetilde{M}|_{\{f \ne 0\}} \simeq (M[f^{-1}]_0)^{\sim}</math>
as sheaves of modules on the affine scheme <math>\{f \ne 0\} = \operatorname{Spec}(R[f^{-1}]_0)</math>;<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|loc=Ch. II, Proposition 5.11.}}</ref> in fact, this defines <math>\widetilde{M}</math> by gluing.

'''Example''': Let ''R''(1) be the graded ''R''-module given by ''R''(1)<sub>''n''</sub> = ''R''<sub>''n''+1</sub>. Then <math>O(1) = \widetilde{R(1)}</math> is called [[Serre's twisting sheaf]], which is the dual of the [[tautological line bundle]] if ''R'' is finitely generated in degree-one.

If ''F'' is an ''O''-module on ''X'', then, writing <math>F(n) = F \otimes O(n)</math>, there is a canonical homomorphism:
:<math>\left(\bigoplus_{n \ge 0} \Gamma(X, F(n))\right)^{\sim} \to F,</math>
which is an isomorphism if and only if ''F'' is quasi-coherent.

== Computing sheaf cohomology ==
{{main|sheaf cohomology}}

Sheaf cohomology has a reputation for being difficult to calculate. Because of this, the next general fact is fundamental for any practical computation:
{{math_theorem|Let ''X'' be a topological space, ''F'' an abelian sheaf on it and <math>\mathfrak{U}</math> an open cover of ''X'' such that <math>\operatorname{H}^i(U_{i_0} \cap \cdots \cap U_{i_p}, F) = 0</math> for any ''i'', ''p'' and <math>U_{i_j}</math>'s in <math>\mathfrak{U}</math>. Then for any ''i'',
:<math>\operatorname{H}^i(X, F) = \operatorname{H}^{i}(C^{\bullet}(\mathfrak{U}, F))</math>
where the right-hand side is the ''i''-th [[Čech cohomology]].}}

[[Serre's vanishing theorem]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Section 30.2 (01X8): Čech cohomology of quasi-coherent sheaves—The Stacks project |url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01X8 |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref> states that if ''X'' is a projective variety and ''F'' a coherent sheaf on it, then, for sufficiently large ''n'', the [[Serre twist]] ''F''(''n'') is generated by finitely many global sections. Moreover,
<ol type="a">
<li> For each ''i'', H<sup>''i''</sup>(''X'', ''F'') is finitely generated over ''R''<sub>0</sub>, and</li>
<li> There is an integer ''n''<sub>0</sub>, depending on ''F'', such that
<math display="block">\operatorname{H}^i(X, F(n)) = 0, \, i \ge 1, n \ge n_0.</math></li>
</ol><ref>{{harvnb|Costa|Miró-Roig|Pons-Llopis|2021|loc=Theorem 1.3.1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1017/CBO9781139044059.023 |chapter=Links with sheaf cohomology |title=Local Cohomology |series=Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics |year=2012 |pages=438–479 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9780521513630 }}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Serre|1955|loc=§.66 Faisceaux algébriques cohérents sur les variétés projectives.}}</ref>

== Sheaf extension ==
Let (''X'', ''O'') be a ringed space, and let ''F'', ''H'' be sheaves of ''O''-modules on ''X''. An '''extension''' of ''H'' by ''F'' is a [[short exact sequence]] of ''O''-modules
:<math>0 \rightarrow F \rightarrow G \rightarrow H \rightarrow 0.</math>

As with group extensions, if we fix ''F'' and ''H'', then all equivalence classes of extensions of ''H'' by ''F'' form an [[abelian group]] (cf. [[Baer sum]]), which is isomorphic to the [[Ext functor|Ext group]] <math>\operatorname{Ext}_O^1(H,F)</math>, where the identity element in <math>\operatorname{Ext}_O^1(H,F)</math> corresponds to the trivial extension.

In the case where ''H'' is ''O'', we have: for any ''i'' ≥ 0,
:<math>\operatorname{H}^i(X, F) = \operatorname{Ext}_O^i(O,F),</math>
since both the sides are the right derived functors of the same functor <math>\Gamma(X, -) = \operatorname{Hom}_O(O, -).</math>

'''Note''': Some authors, notably Hartshorne, drop the subscript ''O''.

Assume ''X'' is a projective scheme over a Noetherian ring. Let ''F'', ''G'' be coherent sheaves on ''X'' and ''i'' an integer. Then there exists ''n''<sub>0</sub> such that
:<math>\operatorname{Ext}_O^i(F, G(n)) = \Gamma(X, \mathcal{Ext}_O^i(F, G(n))), \, n \ge n_0</math>,
where <math>\mathcal{Ext}_O</math> denotes the derived functors of <math>\mathcal{Hom}_O</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|loc=Ch. III, Proposition 6.9.}}</ref>
{{See also|local-to-global Ext spectral sequence}}

=== Locally free resolutions ===
<math>\mathcal{Ext}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G})</math> can be readily computed for any coherent sheaf <math>\mathcal{F}</math> using a locally free [[Resolution (algebra)|resolution]]:<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hartshorne|first1=Robin|title=Algebraic Geometry|pages=233–235}}</ref> given a complex
:<math>
\cdots \to \mathcal{L}_2 \to \mathcal{L}_1 \to \mathcal{L}_0 \to \mathcal{F} \to 0
</math>
then
:<math>
\mathcal{RHom}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}) = \mathcal{Hom}(\mathcal{L}_\bullet,\mathcal{G})
</math>
hence
:<math>\mathcal{Ext}^k(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}) = h^k(\mathcal{Hom}(\mathcal{L}_\bullet,\mathcal{G}))</math>

=== Examples ===

====Hypersurface====
Consider a smooth [[hypersurface]] <math>X</math> of degree <math>d</math>. Then, we can compute a resolution
:<math>\mathcal{O}(-d) \to \mathcal{O}</math>
and find that
:<math>\mathcal{Ext}^i(\mathcal{O}_X,\mathcal{F}) = h^i(\mathcal{Hom}(\mathcal{O}(-d) \to \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{F}))</math>

====Union of smooth complete intersections====
Consider the scheme
:<math>X = \text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]}{(f)(g_1,g_2,g_3)} \right) \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n</math>
where <math>(f,g_1,g_2,g_3)</math> is a smooth [[complete intersection]] and <math>\deg(f) = d</math>, <math>\deg(g_i) = e_i</math>. We have a complex
:<math>
\mathcal{O}(-d-e_1-e_2-e_3) \xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix} g_3 \\ -g_2 \\ -g_1 \end{bmatrix}} \begin{matrix} \mathcal{O}(-d-e_1-e_2) \\ \oplus \\ \mathcal{O}(-d-e_1-e_3) \\ \oplus \\ \mathcal{O}(-d-e_2-e_3) \end{matrix} \xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix} g_2 & g_3 & 0 \\ -g_1 & 0 & -g_3 \\ 0 & -g_1 & g_2 \end{bmatrix}} \begin{matrix} \mathcal{O}(-d-e_1) \\ \oplus \\ \mathcal{O}(-d-e_2) \\ \oplus \\ \mathcal{O}(-d-e_3)  \end{matrix} \xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix} fg_1 & fg_2 & fg_3 \end{bmatrix}} \mathcal{O}
</math>
resolving <math>\mathcal{O}_X,</math> which we can use to compute <math>\mathcal{Ext}^i(\mathcal{O}_X,\mathcal{F})</math>.
